summary: Email can contain private information, and a report about a message may need to hide parts of it before being shared. This RFC suggests one method for redacting sensitive data from mail abuse reports.

eli5.summary: Before sharing a complaint letter, you black out private parts. This says how to do the blacking-out properly.

questions: remove personal data from arf report
how to redact email addresses in arf reports
why not replace the local part with xxxx
subtitle: How to hide who complained in an email abuse report while still letting the receiver spot repeat complaints about the same person.

tldr.problem: Abuse reports about email often contain the address of the user who complained. Replacing it with a fixed string like "xxxxxxxx" protects the user but makes it impossible to group or prioritize reports.
tldr.mechanism: The report generator runs each sensitive string, such as the local-part of an address, through a consistent, collision-resistant transformation and puts the (possibly base64-encoded) result in its place. The same input always gives the same output.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can tell that several reports involve the same hidden user without learning who that is. The RFC stresses this is a privacy measure set by local policy, not strong security.

facts.label: Required transformation
facts.value: None specified; must be consistent and collision-resistant

today: RFC 6590 is a Proposed Standard from April 2012 and, per the metadata for this unit, has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the reporting format in RFC 5965.

sections.title: Why Redact Abuse Reports
sections.content:
The Abuse Reporting Format (ARF, defined in RFC 5965) lets mail systems send automated reports about abusive messages. For privacy, a report generator may want to obscure parts of the report that could identify the end user who caused it, a step that feedback loop operators call redaction. ARF leaves the method to local policy and warns generators not to be overzealous, because hiding too much makes a report non-actionable.

Earlier practice replaced the local-part of addresses with a uniform string such as xxxxxxxx. That frustrated any prioritizing or grouping of reports. This memo describes a way to redact so that a receiver can see that two redacted strings came from identical originals, without revealing the identity.

The RFC assumes recipient-identifying fields are obscured, while other data is left intact and could be correlated against log files to find the intended recipient.
sections.eli5: If every hidden name is covered with the same black bar, you cannot tell whether one kid or ten kids were complaining. This idea gives each kid a different secret nickname so you can tell.

sections.title: The Recommended Practice
sections.content:
When redaction is wanted and the receiver should be able to correlate reports from a common but anonymous source, the generator SHOULD follow five steps.

  1. Select a transformation mechanism that is consistent (the same input always gives the same output) and reasonably collision-resistant (two different inputs are unlikely to give the same output).
  2. Identify the strings in the message that need redacting, for example local-parts of email addresses. The RFC calls these the "private data".
  3. Apply the transformation to each piece of private data.
  4. If the output can contain bytes that are not printable ASCII, or characters unsuitable in that spot, encode it with base64 (RFC 4648) or something similar. For instance, a local-part cannot contain an @ or a space.
  5. Replace each instance of the private data with the matching, possibly encoded, result. The replaced text may sit in a context with limits such as length.

The effect is to obscure the data, possibly irreversibly, while still showing that many reports concern one end user. That lets a receiver prioritize problems that look focused on specific users who may be under attack.
sections.eli5: Pick a nickname-making machine that always gives the same nickname for the same name. Feed it each private name, write the nickname in its place, and make sure the nickname uses only letters that fit.

sections.title: Choosing a Transformation
sections.content:
The memo does not require any particular transformation. The interoperability it seeks comes from the transformation being consistent. How hard it is to reverse is a matter of local policy.

The RFC describes a continuum, from trivial transformations such as rot13, CRC32 and base64, through strong cryptographic encodings such as HMAC and even full encryption, to private mappings such as turning an email address into an internal customer number. An operator should choose one that obscures the data and resists extraction as far as local policy requires, remembering that the environment is not a highly secure one. An implementation MAY choose any transformation with a reasonably low likelihood of collision.
sections.eli5: You can use a simple scrambler or a very strong lock. What matters most is that it scrambles the same name the same way every time.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
General security issues for these reports are covered in ARF. This RFC adds two points. First, digest collisions could make a receiver wrongly decide two redacted strings were originally the same, which could cause unjustified corrective action, a form of denial of service. The RFC calls such cases sufficiently unlikely to be of little concern.

Second, information that is not redacted, such as the Message-ID field, could be used to find the original data in the originating system's logs or through other correlation. The generator should anticipate and redact such data, or accept that recovery is possible. For this reason the normative text makes no stronger claims about cryptography: redaction satisfies a privacy requirement set by local policy and is not meant to provide strong security.

On privacy, the RFC notes that it is extremely unlikely software could recognize every way private information can be expressed in human written language. Where more protection is needed, implementers may consider out-of-band arrangements between the entities involved. Bilateral agreements between report producers and consumers (RFC 6449 and ARF) raise related issues.
sections.eli5: A nickname hides the name, but if you leave other clues lying around, a clever detective can still work out who it was. So hide the clues too, or accept that someone might find out.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
An email from alice@example.com to bob@example.net with the subject "Make money fast!" is reported as abusive by Bob. The domain example.net wants to hide Bob's address so it is not relayed to the offending sender.

Local policy picks the keyed hash "H" (a hash of a key concatenated with the data) using SHA1. The redaction key is potatoes and the private data is bob. The string potatoesbob is digested with SHA1 and base64-encoded, giving rZ8cqXWGiKHzhz1MsFRGTysHia4=. In the ARF report, the To field becomes rZ8cqXWGiKHzhz1MsFRGTysHia4=@example.net.

The RFC then points out that agents at example.com could still recover the address by searching logs and matching the unredacted Message-ID. It expects feedback loops that generate such reports to involve senders vetted against that kind of leakage.
sections.eli5: Bob's name is mixed with a secret word and turned into a long jumble. The jumble goes where his name was. It is the same jumble every time, but nobody can read Bob's name from it.
